extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (Korean Patent Office / Korea)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on determining inventive step (obviousness) and the enlarged concept of novelty (Article 29(3)-(6)) under the Korean Patent Act, including how to treat combinations of prior art, secondary evidence, priority/divisional/international application issues, and exceptions. Intended to direct examiners' evaluation and rejection/grant decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation / substitution leading to obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If modification or substitution of elements does not lead to structural difficulties and the functional effect of new elements is not regarded as greater than the summed effects of the prior art references, the claimed invention falls within an aggregation and is therefore denied inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: substituting a spindle from prior art reference 2 for the spindle of prior art reference 1 — if no structural difficulties and no greater functional effect, treat as aggregation. Examiner should assess whether summed effects are merely additive rather than producing a remarkable effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation in multiple-reference combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claimed invention corresponds to a combination of elements disclosed across multiple prior art references, if the combination does not lead to particular difficulties nor produce any remarkable difference in functional effect, the aggregation is considered obvious to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: combining an injection molding machine, a vacuum chamber, and a mold fastening system — if combination is straightforward and effect unremarkable, it is obvious. Examiner should evaluate whether the combination causes particular technical difficulties or a remarkable synergistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care in combining prior art references (three-factor test)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether it would have been obvious to combine two or more prior arts, the examiner should consider: ① good possibility that a person of ordinary skill would combine them, ② whether the prior arts come from similar or neighboring technical fields, and ③ whether there is a reasonable basis to associate them with each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also note that relying on a large number of prior art references may indicate improper hindsight or an invalid ground for rejection. Combination should not be presumed without showing why a skilled person would make the association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthetic determination of inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step determination should consider synthetically the objective, technical configuration, and functional effect of an invention described in a claim — i.e., the uniqueness of the objective and the remarkableness of the effect as a whole, mainly based on the difficulty of technical configuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not readily conclude lack of inventive step if applicant offers written arguments claiming non-obviousness; consider other supportive factors (teaching away, secondary evidence, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away (prior art discouraging the claimed approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art reference teaches not to rely on the prior art thereof (i.e., contains a description that teaches away from the claimed invention), the inventive step is not denied by that prior art despite similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, mere description of a prior art as 'inferior' is not necessarily teaching away. Examiner must identify explicit discouragement or negative guidance in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success as secondary evidence (limited weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success or favorable industry comments, or the fact that the invention had not been implemented for a long time before filing, may be regarded as indicative of inventive step as secondary evidence; however, these facts alone are not sufficient to establish inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success must derive from the technical features of the invention, not from sales techniques, advertising, or other non-technical factors. Objective linkage between technical features and success is required. Examples illustrate when success did not prove inventive step because success derived from marketing rather than technical superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need or attempted long-standing solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed invention solves a technical problem that skilled persons have attempted to solve for a long time, or fulfills a long-felt need, this may indicate inventive step, provided the claimed invention is the first to fulfill the need and objective evidence is presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require objective evidence showing prior attempts and that the claimed solution is a recognized first fulfillment by skilled persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of abandoned technical means due to prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention employs technical means that skilled persons had abandoned due to technical prejudice (which interfered with R&D) and thereby solves the technical problem, this is regarded as an indicator of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the technical means were truly abandoned for non-trivial reasons and whether the claimed invention overcomes those prejudices to solve the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming otherwise irresolvable technical difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed invention proposes means for overcoming technical difficulties not resolvable by other means or for solving a technical problem, this is regarded as advantageous evidence for an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the technical difficulties were indeed intractable by known approaches and whether the claimed means provide an inventive solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand-new technology / lack of relevant prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed invention falls within the area of a brand-new technology and has no prior art relevant to the invention, or if the closest prior art is far removed from the invention, the inventive step is likely to be recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the technological gap between prior art and claimed invention; lack of relevant prior art strengthens inventive-step finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding improper hindsight (using specification knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining inventive step in light of knowledge obtained from the application under examination (the specification), the examiner should avoid rapidly concluding the invention would have been obvious — using the application's disclosure to show obviousness can be improper hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a specification describing a 'tapping mode' should not be retrofitted to a vague prior-art teaching 'preventing others from noticing voice reception' to argue obviousness. Use objective technical similarities, not knowledge of applicant's disclosure, to assess obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims inherit inventive step from inventive independent claim
rubrics_metrics.description: If an independent claim involves an inventive step, a claim dependent on the independent claim is deemed to involve an inventive step too. If the independent claim lacks inventive step, the examiner must assess each dependent claim individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically reject or accept dependents without separate consideration when independent lacks inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claim implies process/use inventive step (principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a product invention explicitly involves an inventive step, a process invention for making the product or a use invention for using the product also involves an inventive step in principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a general principle but assess case-by-case where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush-type and multiple-alternative claims caution
rubrics_metrics.description: For Markush-type claims or claims reciting multiple alternative technical features, if at least one alternative is proved to lack inventive step based on prior art, the applicant may be notified and can overcome rejection by deleting the lacking alternatives. Care must be taken not to expand the effect of one alternative to the whole claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In chemical Markush claims, every alternative must show remarkable effect over prior art; granting based on a single effective alternative is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degenerate invention lacks inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: A degenerate invention does not involve an inventive step; granting a patent to a degenerate invention is contrary to the purpose of the Patent Act and may negatively affect users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should identify degenerate inventions (those that are barely conducted or have negative effect) and treat them as lacking inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-known technology can support rejection but needs evidential support if disputed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art reference is regarded as a well-known technology, the examiner may notify rejection without attaching evidentiary material; however, it is inappropriate to regard something as well-known without evidence. If the applicant disputes well-known status, the examiner should provide evidential material or fully explain why the art is well-known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials that disclose well-known technology include widely-used textbooks, introductory books, technical standards dictionaries, national standards (KS), etc. Be cautious in rapidly-evolving fields (e.g., ICT) where standards dictionaries may not reflect well-known status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign examination results are non-binding (case-by-case determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of inventive step should not be affected by examination results of precedents for other inventions in different cases. Examination results in foreign countries may be a reference but are not binding and do not need to be followed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat foreign outcomes only as informative; analyze the current case's facts and legal standard independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law restrictions irrelevant to inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementation prohibitions or legal restrictions on the technical content of the claimed invention (domestically or abroad) are not taken into consideration when determining inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a lottery-drawing method prohibited by law is still assessed on technical difficulty alone and considered obvious if technically straightforward, despite legal prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess prior art by whole disclosure (no cherry-picking)
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining obviousness in view of prior art, the examiner should base the decision on matters a person skilled in the art can reasonably recognize from the whole disclosure of the prior art, rather than certain parts which might unfairly constitute a ground for lack of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an applicant presents other prior art that contradicts parts of the disclosure or makes them unclear, the examiner should comprehensively determine whether a skilled person can easily arrive at the claimed invention by considering the prior art as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlarged concept of novelty — Article 29(3)-(6): basic conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention shall not be patentable if it is identical to an invention described in the specification or drawings as originally filed in another patent application that: 1) was filed prior to the present application's filing date, and 2) was laid open to the public or published/registered after the present application was filed. Similarly applies for utility model applications under conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The present application's inventor/applicant exceptions apply. This rule prevents later applicants from gaining rights to what was already disclosed in another application's original filing. See special treatments for international applications and translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 29 — identity of invention requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention described in the claims of the present application should be completely or substantially identical to an invention or utility innovation described in the original specification of another application for Article 29(3)-(4) to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the matters in the original specification of another application are later omitted by amendment, Article 29(3,4) is implemented. Examiner must assess substantial identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 29 — filing date and priority handling (divisional/converted and Paris priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Another application must have been filed before the present filing date. For divisional or converted applications, the effective filing date is the actual filing date of the divisional/converted application (they do not have retroactive effect). For applications with Paris Convention priority, the filing date in the first country is deemed the filing date of the 'another application' for inventions commonly disclosed in both filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a divisional filed after the present application's filing cannot be cited as prior art under Article 29(3,4), but the original application may be. For priority cases, only inventions disclosed in the first-country filing are considered for the earlier date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of prior-filed vs later-filed applications with domestic priority (common disclosure rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on inventions disclosed in the original specification of a prior-filed application that formed the basis for a domestic priority claim and a later-filed application, (a) inventions commonly disclosed in both are deemed another application filed on the filing date of the prior-filed application and apply under Article 29(3,4); (b) inventions solely in the later-filed application's original specification are deemed filed on the later-filed application's date; inventions solely in the prior-filed application's original specification but not in later-filed are not applied under Article 29(3,4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior-filed application is deemed withdrawn if not laid open after certain periods (e.g., 1 year 3 months) — timing affects lay-open status. If invention was newly described via amendment, these rules do not apply. Examples clarify which inventions can be relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception — same inventor(s) of present and another application
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor(s) of the present application are the same as those of another application (as indicated on application cover sheets), the application is not considered 'another application' under Article 29(3)-(6). For joint inventions, all inventors must completely coincide, though practical equivalence can be proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant amends inventors after a rejection based on another application, they have the right to request documents proving the added/amended inventors are true inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception — same applicant(s) of present and another application
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant of the present application at filing is the same as the applicant of another application, then the other application is not considered 'another application' under Article 29(3)-(6). For plural applicants, all applicants must match; subsequent changes (name changes, inheritance, merger) are considered for substantial sameness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner compares applicants as of the filing date of the present application to determine sameness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special rules for international (PCT) applications and translations
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'another application' is an international application, 'laid open' may include international publication under PCT Article 21. The scope of inventions applied under Article 29 varies depending on filing dates (pre/post Dec 31, 2014 / Jan 1, 2015). For applications filed on/after Jan 1, 2015, if the applicant fails to submit a Korean translation within the specified period under Article 201(4), the international application may be deemed withdrawn and cannot be relied upon as another application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where international applications claim domestic priority, inventions disclosed in the specification/claims/drawings submitted at the international filing date and translations determine the extent of enlarged novelty application. Examiner must pay attention to whether translations exist and which documents were submitted at which filing date.
